summary:
Delta State stands under Nigeria's national framework, and no state-specific protective statute exists in Delta. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act applies in the state with up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex unions, and the death penalty attached to Shari'a provisions is confined to the twelve northern states, none of which is Delta.

Enforcement in Delta has taken the form of mass arrests at social venues. In June 2018 police in Asaba arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel on charges that they were gays and lesbians; by July 2018 the detainees were facing homosexuality-related charges in court.

On 27 August 2023 officers of the Ekpan Division, Uvwie Local Government Area, raided Teebolus Hotel on Refinery Road, Ekpan, in Warri at 9 pm and arrested 67 suspects for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between a 22-year-old groom and a 20-year-old bride. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a confession by a male cross-dresser that he belonged to a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that suspects fled on the officers' arrival and 67 were chased down, and that drugs and what police called gay marriage ceremonial dresses were recovered. He said efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution. One suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. The case is known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court.

Accounts of the same August 2023 operation differ. The US State Department's 2023 human rights report, cited in the UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy note, records that police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organised by the LGBTQI+ community on 27 August 2023 and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account.

A human rights lawyer based in Warri told the Home Office that victims of 'kito' — predatory same-sex assault — under-report for fear of prosecution, which leaves the extortion and violence risk in Delta largely unrecorded.
tangentialFactors:
Delta's documented enforcement actions are framed by police together with drug allegations: the Warri raid was announced alongside the recovery of drugs and ceremonial clothing, a framing that broadens the charges beyond the same-sex conduct itself and hardens the public account of the event.

The figures reported for the 27 August 2023 operation do not reconcile across sources. Daily Post and the police command give 67 arrested and charged at Teebolus Hotel; the US State Department account gives more than 200 detained at a 'white party' the same night, with civil society disputing the police characterisation of the event as a same-sex wedding. Both figures are reported here as they stand.

The trigger for the Warri raid was a confession attributed to a detained cross-dresser, which places gender presentation at the centre of how the operation was justified and indicates that police in Delta treat cross-dressing and attendance at the same venue as connected grounds for a raid.
localsOnly:
Residents of Delta State have no state-level legal protection against discrimination or violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the national statute is applied by the Delta State Police Command as ordinary law, with public statements from its spokesman naming suspects and the alleged nature of the ceremony.

Those arrested in Delta face protracted court proceedings: the Asaba defendants were still facing homosexuality-related charges in court by July 2018, several months after the June 2018 raid, and the 67 Warri defendants were charged following the August 2023 operation.

Warri-based legal and human rights practitioners report that victims of 'kito' assault do not come forward because reporting risks prosecution under the same framework, so assault, extortion and blackmail against Delta residents are handled outside the formal system where they are handled at all.
outOfScopeNotes:
State-level documentation for Delta is thin, and thin documentation does not demonstrate safety; the two raids above are the incidents the sources carry, not an enumeration of enforcement in the state.

The discrepancy between the 67 charged and the more than 200 detained accounts of 27 August 2023 is unresolved in the sources available, as is whether the two accounts describe one operation or two separate actions that night.

Outcomes are not sourced: whether the Asaba defendants were convicted, and what happened to the 67 Warri defendants after charging, are not documented in the material reviewed. The allegation of sexual assault made by one Warri suspect has no recorded follow-up.
